cards.title: Feed-Only Performance Max as a Remarketing Layer Behind Shopping
cards.summary: Configure PMAX with an empty asset group so it serves only Shopping feed listings, positioned as a retargeting follow-up to a new-customer acquisition Shopping campaign.
cards.use_when: Restructuring Google Ads for an established store that already has consistent conversions and wants a PMAX campaign that retargets product viewers rather than cannibalizing new-customer acquisition.
steps: Confirm prerequisites before building: Merchant Center linked and clean, an existing non-branded Shopping campaign driving new customers, and enough conversion data to identify best-performing products (the source places this around step two of account maturity).
Create a new campaign: Sales objective, purchases as conversion goal, Performance Max type. Name it by convention that encodes geo, purpose and focus, e.g. 'PMax USA feed only remarketing focus'.

At the asset stage, delete everything: no final URL, headlines, descriptions, logos, images or videos. Every asset box must be completely blank, otherwise Google blocks continuation with 'please add all assets'. This is what forces the campaign to rely solely on the Shopping feed.

Leave audience signals empty. The source's stated position is that signals often steer PMAX away from high-intent customers and that community consensus is PMAX usually performs slightly better without them; treat this as the presenter's observation, not a universal law.
Set bidding to Maximize conversion value rather than a tROAS target, because this campaign exists to extract more value from traffic the Shopping campaign already generated.
Turn off automatically created assets wherever offered, to preserve control over what is shown.
Set the non-branded Shopping campaign to High priority in campaign settings. This is what makes the structure work: product searches are served by the Shopping campaign, and PMAX picks up the rest.

Exclude brand traffic from PMAX via a negative keyword list (brand name and variants, exact match). Because PMAX lacks a self-serve negative-list UI, request the list be applied through the Google support form linked in the platform; verify this interface still works as shown.
Keep branded traffic isolated in branded Shopping/branded Search campaigns so attribution stays clean.
caveats: This setup only works alongside a correctly structured new-customer Shopping campaign; it is not a standalone configuration.
Negative keyword list application in PMAX may require a support request and could change as Google updates the interface.
The 'signals hurt PMAX' claim is the presenter's experience and cited community consensus, not a proven rule.

cards.title: Excluding Branded Traffic from PMAX to Protect Attribution
cards.summary: Build a negative keyword list of brand terms and apply it to PMAX so brand demand stays in branded Shopping and Search campaigns and PMAX only handles non-branded remarketing.
cards.use_when: Merchandising/measurement decision when PMAX is absorbing branded searches and inflating its apparent results while muddying which campaign actually drives new customers.
steps: Confirm you already run a separate branded Shopping campaign (and branded Search) that captures brand demand; this is the precondition for excluding brand from PMAX.
In the PMAX campaign, go to Audiences, keywords and content, then Search keywords, then Negative search keywords.
Add every brand variant customers might search, in exact match: brand name, brand plus product category, common misspellings and product-specific brand phrases.
Save them into a new shared negative keyword list named for brand exclusion so the same list can be reused across campaigns.

Because PMAX does not allow you to attach the list directly in the UI (as described in this course), use the Google support form to request the negative keyword list be applied to the PMAX campaign. Verify the current application method before relying on it.
Assign roles in reporting: branded Shopping and branded Search collect branded traffic only; non-branded Shopping drives new customers; PMAX catches past visitors and non-converting traffic.
Re-audit search terms periodically to identify new brand variants to add.
caveats: Requires an existing branded campaign structure; excluding brand without one loses brand traffic entirely.
The support-form route for applying negatives to PMAX is the presenter's workaround at time of recording and may be outdated.

cards.title: Deciding Between Feed-Only PMAX and Asset-Filled PMAX
cards.summary: Choose feed-only PMAX when you already run a non-branded Shopping campaign, and understand the trade-offs of the standard all-assets PMAX that substitutes for it.
cards.use_when: Campaign architecture decision for a store deciding whether PMAX should carry new-customer acquisition or only retarget, based on whether a non-branded Shopping campaign already exists.
steps: If you run a properly structured non-branded Shopping campaign: use feed-only PMAX as a remarketing layer, and do not add assets. The source describes this as the most efficient current setup for ecommerce.

If you have no non-branded Shopping campaign: the standard all-assets PMAX (best-seller products, filled headlines/descriptions/images/video) can act as a substitute, but the source does not recommend it.

When building the all-assets version, select best-seller products by item ID or category, then supply a final URL, engaging headlines combining offer, trust and a bold claim (the source's examples include discount framing and customer-count proof), long headlines, descriptions, images and optionally video.

Expect the all-assets PMAX to lean heavily on retargeting and branded traffic. The source warns it will likely show a better ROAS while acquiring fewer new customers, so judge it on new-customer volume, not blended ROAS alone.
Apply the same brand-exclusion negative keyword list to either version.
Treat the source's efficiency judgment as its opinion: it says feed-only is more efficient and gives more data, but presents no controlled test.
caveats: Do not run the all-assets PMAX alongside an existing non-branded Shopping campaign per the source; they overlap and the PMAX will typically consume warm/branded traffic.
The all-assets version gives less granular insight into where spend goes.

cards.title: Budgeting and Sequencing Demand Gen Campaigns
cards.summary: Sequence Demand Gen as the top-of-funnel step after PMAX, and allocate on the order of 30% of account budget when new-customer acquisition is the priority.
cards.use_when: Budget and rollout planning for a store deciding when to add Demand Gen and how much daily spend to commit relative to its existing Shopping/PMAX setup.
steps: Decide timing by budget: with a smaller budget and no proof on other platforms, implement Demand Gen after PMAX remarketing. With a high budget, existing proof on other platforms, and rapid scaling goals, implement it alongside PMAX (source treats this as step two versus step three).
Set the campaign as Sales objective, purchases conversion goal, Demand Gen campaign type.
Use best-seller products as the starting product set so the campaign accumulates data quickly and can be tested and iterated fast.
Enable the product feed with your Merchant Center account so catalog items appear alongside the video/image ads and shorten the path to purchase.

Start with conversion-based bidding and leave target CPA unchecked; the source argues you cannot know a realistic CPA before the campaign has data, and a misaligned target slows learning. Switch to conversion value bidding only if the account already has results to support it.

Set daily budget relative to AOV: the source's illustration is roughly $50/day at $10–20 AOV and $100+/day at around $50 AOV, and it recommends allocating about 30% of the full account budget to Demand Gen when focused on new customers (e.g. ~$150/day out of a $500/day account). Treat these as starting heuristics, not benchmarks.
Expect to invest meaningfully: the source states these campaigns need real budget to generate conversions.
caveats: Budget figures are the presenter's rough guidance tied to AOV and total budget, not tested benchmarks.
Converting new customers at '2+ ROAS' on cold traffic is presented as an observed example, not a promise.

cards.title: Demand Gen Setup: Settings, Placements and Device Controls
cards.summary: Configure Demand Gen location, device and partner settings to keep spend on higher-quality placements and, where desired, bias video delivery toward Shorts.
cards.use_when: Technical setup of a Demand Gen campaign for a store that wants control over placement quality and format, especially when repurposing short-form social creatives.
steps: Set location and language at campaign level (or ad group level if you need variation). The source's example targets the US with English.
Disable Google video partners. The source compares them to low-quality display/search network placements and says results are worse than standard Google placements.
If you want to bias toward YouTube Shorts, narrow devices to mobile only. The source notes this increases the chance of Shorts placement but cannot guarantee it.

Understand the format selection caveat: if you assign a video only to Shorts, Google requires at least one video showing in each format for that choice to fully apply, and the source's observation is that it may still serve the video in other formats (in-stream, in-feed).
Turn off video enhancements so Google does not auto-edit your creatives into formats that may crop content or wording.
Note that device narrowing plus Shorts targeting together is the best available control for Shorts-specific delivery in the source's experience.
caveats: Format selection behavior is described as unclear in Google's documentation and the source's read is an assumption based on observed data.
Verify current placement and enhancement settings in the live interface, as these change frequently.

cards.title: Structuring Demand Gen Ad Groups by Creative Theme
cards.summary: Split Demand Gen ad groups by creative theme (e.g. UGC product reviews) and keep image and product creatives in separate ad groups or campaigns for clean testing.
cards.use_when: Creative and ad-group planning when launching Demand Gen for a store that has multiple creative concepts or formats to test against a product set.
steps: Group creatives by theme, not by randomness: for example, one ad group containing three to five iterations of a UGC-style product review video for a specific product.

Pair each theme ad group with the matching product selection, e.g. select the specific item IDs for the stainless steel pans being reviewed, so creatives and catalog items stay relevant to each other.
Run video ads first. The source states video is the most effective and highest-return Demand Gen format it has seen, especially when you have proven Meta/TikTok/Snapchat creatives to port over.
Separate image ads (image + products format) into their own ad group, and consider a separate campaign; do not mix them into the video ad group.
Treat product ads as separate again, at minimum a distinct ad group. The source notes these are very new and it has limited data, so treat as experimental.
Point each ad to the most relevant URL: the specific product page when the ad promotes one product, or a relevant category/landing page when it covers a range.
Do not reuse another creator's YouTube video as your own ad creative; the source's example of pulling a random Short is illustrative only.
caveats: The claim that video is the highest-return format is the presenter's observation, not a benchmark.
Product ads are new with thin data in the source; results may differ.

cards.title: Keeping Demand Gen Assets Few and Varied Enough to Test
cards.summary: Limit headlines/descriptions to one to three high-quality options per ad so split tests remain interpretable instead of exploding into untraceable combinations.
cards.use_when: Creative testing decision for a store setting up Demand Gen (or similar) ads that wants to know which messaging actually drives conversions.
steps: Fill only the fields that apply to the chosen format and keep optional asset counts low: the source recommends roughly one to three headlines, descriptions and long headlines for Demand Gen assets.
Recognize the combinatorial problem: five of each field multiplies into combinations you cannot attribute, making it impossible to know which headline performed.
Run identical ad content with only a single variable changed between ads so you can compare cleanly, rather than changing several fields at once.
Keep the copy extremely relevant to the specific product or theme of the ad group, and high quality over quantity.
Note that this low-count guidance is specific to Demand Gen-style assets; the source separately notes Search ads require at least three headlines, so do not apply the 'one to three' rule to Search.
caveats: Minimum asset counts differ by campaign type; check current platform requirements.
Single-variable testing assumes sufficient volume for significance; the source does not address low-volume cases.

cards.title: Audience Signals in Demand Gen: Bias Toward Cold Reach
cards.summary: Leave Demand Gen targeting open or use a few in-market/search-theme signals, but never import your own customer or remarketing lists, which pushes it toward warm traffic.
cards.use_when: Targeting setup for a Demand Gen campaign when the goal is new-customer acquisition and you must avoid duplicating remarketing already handled by PMAX.
steps: Default to fully open targeting: the source reports this performs best for its Demand Gen campaigns.

If you do add signals, use external interest indicators only: roughly three to five search themes, one to two in-market segments, and a couple of demographic adjustments, kept conservative so testing stays interpretable.

Never include your own data: no customer lists, remarketing audiences, or converter audiences, since these direct Google toward people who already know the brand, which defeats the new-customer purpose.
Avoid affinity segments; the source considers them too broad and low-meaning.
Turn off optimized targeting. The source says it makes targeting go wide in ways that produce lower-quality traffic; testing it later is optional once you have results.
Test with and without signals to see which your account responds to, rather than assuming signals help.
caveats: The 'open targeting performs best' finding is the presenter's campaign experience, not a controlled benchmark.
Audience options and naming may change in Google's interface.

cards.title: Assigning Funnel Roles Across the Google Ads Account
cards.summary: Map each campaign type to a funnel job — Shopping/Search for new and branded demand, Display/YouTube for remarketing, PMAX for product remarketing, Demand Gen for top-of-funnel cold reach.
cards.use_when: Whole-account architecture review for a store unsure whether campaigns are duplicating work, cannibalizing each other, or leaving a funnel stage uncovered.
steps: Assign non-branded Shopping as the new-customer acquisition driver; exclude past visitors and branded traffic there so it targets genuinely new buyers.
Assign branded Shopping and branded Search purely to collecting branded demand, nothing else.
Assign Display and YouTube remarketing to re-engage site visitors.
Assign Performance Max to product remarketing and follow-up: catching past visitors, branded-adjacent and non-converting traffic the Shopping campaign does not target.
Assign Demand Gen to the top of funnel: capturing new users and traffic on YouTube, Discover and Gmail, the closest Google surfaces to Meta/TikTok-style cold acquisition.
Sequence implementation: Shopping and branded campaigns first, then PMAX remarketing once conversions are consistent, then Demand Gen (or alongside PMAX if you have budget and scaling ambition).
Check each new campaign against this map before launch to confirm it does not duplicate another campaign's traffic.
caveats: The exact role boundaries depend on having separate branded and non-branded campaigns; without them, roles blur.
The source presents this as its recommended structure for ecommerce, not the only valid one.

cards.title: Pre-Launch Checklist for Google Ads Campaign Settings
cards.summary: A short checklist of settings the source disables or verifies across PMAX and Demand Gen: auto-created assets, video enhancements, optimized targeting, video partners and video format coverage.
cards.use_when: Final QA before launching or editing a PMAX or Demand Gen campaign in a store's account, to avoid giving Google uncontrolled creative and placement decisions.
steps: Turn off automatically created assets in every campaign where the option appears; the source's rationale is that auto-created assets mean you don't know what is shown or what you are paying for, and it explicitly skips the asset-generation screens.
Remove auto-populated assets (logos, final URLs) when building a feed-only PMAX, since even one residual asset breaks the feed-only requirement.
Turn off video enhancements in Demand Gen so Google does not reformat your creative.
Disable Google video partners in Demand Gen to avoid lower-quality placements.
Turn off optimized targeting in Demand Gen unless testing it deliberately after results exist.
Accept the red warning boxes Google shows when assets are missing; the source's position is that they are pressure to add assets, not a requirement for the feed-only strategy.
Keep the source's underlying principle: maximize control over what is shown and where, and only delegate control when you can observe the results.
caveats: These are the presenter's control-first preferences, presented as opinion; some accounts may benefit from automation, which the source acknowledges only for targeting in specific cases.
Option locations and names in Google Ads change; verify in the current interface.
